content.title: Triangle Interior–Exterior Angle Relationship
content.overview: This lesson covers the Exterior Angle Theorem, which relates the measure of an exterior angle of a triangle to its two nonadjacent (remote) interior angles. Mastering this relationship allows for faster solving of geometry problems without needing to calculate the adjacent interior angle first.
learning_objectives: Identify exterior angles and their corresponding remote interior angles.
Apply the Exterior Angle Theorem to solve for unknown angle measures.
Differentiate between adjacent interior angles and remote interior angles.

sections.title: Defining the Exterior Angle Theorem
sections.content: An exterior angle is formed when one side of a triangle is extended. The Exterior Angle Theorem states that the measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the measures of its two remote interior angles. Remote interior angles (also called nonadjacent interior angles) are the two angles inside the triangle that do not share a vertex with the exterior angle.

sections.title: The Algebraic Relationship
sections.content: If we extend side BC of triangle ABC to a point D, the angle formed (∠ACD) is the exterior angle. The two remote interior angles are ∠A and ∠B. The relationship is expressed as: Exterior Angle = Remote Interior 1 + Remote Interior 2. Algebraically, this is written as m∠ACD = m∠A + m∠B. This theorem is a shortcut derived from the fact that the sum of interior angles is 180° and the exterior angle forms a linear pair (180°) with its adjacent interior angle.

sections.title: The Exterior-Angle Subtract Strategy
sections.content:
When an ACT problem provides an exterior angle and one remote interior angle, you can find the missing remote interior angle by subtracting the known interior angle from the exterior angle. Step 1: Identify the exterior angle. Step 2: Identify the two remote interior angles. Step 3: Set up the equation (Exterior = Sum of Remotes). Step 4: Solve for the variable.

![A flowchart showing the steps to solve for a remote interior angle: Identify Exterior, Identify Remotes, Set Up Equation, Solve.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/3a8b735a-63a8-4c1f-9563-fca4f08af5fc-1786505957693-117.webp)

worked_examples.question: In triangle ABC, side BC is extended to point D to form an exterior angle ∠ACD measuring 125°. If the measure of interior angle ∠A is 40°, what is the measure of interior angle ∠B?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the exterior angle, which is 125°. Step 2: Identify the remote interior angles, which are ∠A and ∠B. Step 3: Apply the theorem: 125° = ∠A + ∠B. Step 4: Substitute the known value: 125° = 40° + ∠B. Step 5: Subtract 40° from 125° to find ∠B. 125 - 40 = 85. Therefore, ∠B = 85°.

common_mistakes: Confusing the adjacent interior angle with a remote interior angle.
Subtracting the exterior angle from 180° and stopping there (this only finds the adjacent interior angle).
Assuming the exterior angle is equal to just one of the interior angles rather than their sum.
exam_tips: Look for 'extended' lines in geometry diagrams; these almost always create exterior angles.
If you forget the theorem, remember that the exterior angle and the adjacent interior angle must add up to 180°.
Always verify your answer by ensuring the two remote interior angles sum exactly to the exterior angle measure.
content.recap: The measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is exactly equal to the sum of the two remote (nonadjacent) interior angles. Use the formula Exterior = Remote1 + Remote2 to solve for missing values efficiently.

knowledge_claims.content: An exterior angle of a triangle is formed by extending one of the triangle's sides.
The measure of an exterior angle is equal to the sum of the two remote interior angles.
Remote interior angles are the two angles inside a triangle that are not adjacent to a specific exterior angle.
For an exterior angle E and remote interior angles A and B, the relationship is E = A + B.
To find a missing remote interior angle, subtract the known remote interior angle from the exterior angle.
An exterior angle is always greater than either of its individual remote interior angles.
The sum of an exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle must always be 180 degrees.
A common error is incorrectly using the adjacent interior angle in the sum instead of the two remote angles.
In ACT diagrams, a straight line extending past a triangle vertex indicates the presence of an exterior angle.
If an exterior angle is 110° and one remote interior angle is 30°, the other remote interior angle must be 80°.
The Exterior Angle Theorem is a direct consequence of the Triangle Sum Theorem and the definition of supplementary angles.
When solving for an exterior angle, first identify which two interior angles do not share the vertex where the side was extended.
